newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Coffee extends slide, zinc zooms ahead.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Coffee extends slide, zinc zooms ahead.

text.p: World coffee prices modestly extended their slide on Thursday after heavy overnight losses in New York on forecasts of warmer weather in Brazil's coffee belt.
But they managed to regain some lost territory and safely climbed off session lows.

On other commodity markets, zinc turned in a powerful early performance when it jumped to a 4-3/4 year high on speculative buying while copper inched upwards before slinking away from the important psychological barrier of $2,600 per tonne.

Nickel slipped slightly after Inco Ltd. said it would resume talks on Thursday with union officials representing 4,670 striking workers at one of its Canadian mines. A company spokesman said it expected an agreement to be reached over the weekend.
The London coffee market was underpinned by a general lack of sellers, particularly Indonesian origin ones, which prompted talk that the Indonesian crop could be considerably lower than expected.

But warmer temperatures continue to be forecast in the southern hemisphere, where the winter months of June and July are typically the most dangerous for freezing conditions, particularly in the world's largest producer, Brazil.
Benchmark London robusta coffee futures ended the day down just $5 on the September contract at $1,860 per tonne.
Elsewhere, precious metals had a mixed day with much of the action occurring in palladium and platinum, which received a positive jolt on reports of borrowing from the Far East.

Possible central bank gold sales continued to dog the market, particularly after Belgium announced a proposal late on Wednesday to sell 26 tonnes a year of its reserves for a total of five years in the form of commemorative coins.
Gold suffered late in the day to end lower in London at $339.25 per ounce versus $340.85 on Wednesday.
World grain markets had much to chew on during the first day of a two-day gathering of the 44 leading grain importing and exporting nations at the International Grains Council's annual meeting.

The United States sparred with the European Union, warning that it would not agree to segregating genetically modified commodities for separate labels, which the European Commission on Wednesday ruled mandatory after July 31.
U.S. wheat futures slipped on continuing expectations of a strong harvest, with the July contract on the Chicago Board of Trade off 1-1/4 cents at $3.37.

Crude oil turned slightly positive and consolidated after coming under heavy pressure on Wednesday on a view that an OPEC meeting in Vienna next weke would do nothing to curb quota violations. Benchmark London Brent for August delivery was up 13 cents at $17.90.
